title: What Inflation Is and Where It Comes From
text:
Let me clear up a confusion that surfaces whenever inflation is discussed. Inflation is not the same thing as goods being expensive. It is a sustained rise in the general level of prices, which means that the same sum of money buys less as time passes. A single price rising tells you something about one market. Inflation is the whole scale shifting.

Where does it come from? Broadly speaking, from two directions. Demand may run ahead of what the economy is able to produce, so buyers compete for a limited quantity of goods and bid prices upward. Alternatively, costs may rise across the board, as when energy or imported materials become dearer, and firms pass those costs on to their customers. Both push prices up, but they pull output in opposite directions, which is why the second kind is the harder to respond to. What makes inflation persistent is expectation. If workers and firms expect prices to go on climbing, wage demands and price lists are set with that in mind, and the expectation fulfils itself. Moderate and predictable inflation is manageable. What damages an economy is inflation that is high, volatile, or no longer trusted to settle anywhere in particular.
points: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general price level, not simply prices being high.
It means the same money buys less over time; one price rising is not inflation.
Demand can outrun what the economy can produce, so buyers bid prices up.
Costs such as energy or imported materials can rise and be passed on, raising prices while reducing output, which is harder to deal with.
Expectations make inflation persistent, because wages and prices are set in anticipation of it and the expectation fulfils itself.
Moderate, predictable inflation is manageable; high, volatile or untrusted inflation is the damaging kind.
